title: Silt Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Silt wells have a 116 ft median depth, 14 gpm median yield, and estimated finished-well costs of $11,800-$20,700.
h1: What Silt, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Silt means looking past the presence of a well permit. The local record shows 2,364 permitted wells within 5 miles, but only 559 report a pump yield and 197 report a static water level. That makes the available numbers useful for setting expectations, not a guarantee for a particular lot.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and the wells are commonly associated with unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. Nearby Rifle, New Castle and Chacra can provide broader local context, but the well on the property and the wells closest to it matter most.

sections.heading: Silt well depth: mostly shallow to moderate
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Silt is 116 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 180 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site should be thinking in that general range rather than assuming every well reaches several hundred feet. Fifty-seven percent of reported depths fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 37% are under 100 feet.

The spread still matters. The 90th-percentile depth is 240 feet, and the deepest record reaches 750 feet. Local geology is listed mostly as unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 2,311 wells in that category. Alluvial and Wasatch-Fort Union wells are much less common. A nearby well log helps identify the formation, casing and grout conditions a new bid may encounter.

sections.heading: How much water a Silt well can produce
sections.html:
Reported pump yields have a 14.0 gallons-per-minute median, with the middle half between 5.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-eight percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 33% fall between 5 and 15. That is generally a workable range for a household, but yield is not the same as storage or guaranteed long-term supply.

Low-producing wells are part of the local record: 18% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 2% report under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the driller’s yield test, recovery information and pump setting before relying on a listing’s water claims. An exempt household-use well still has Colorado limits, including the 35 gpm pumping limit, and some basins require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Silt water levels and the measured trend
sections.html:
The reported median static water level is 30 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 16 and 51 feet. That can reduce pumping lift compared with a much deeper water level, but it does not tell you how much water the formation can deliver. Water level should be checked at the individual well, preferably before and after pumping.

The decade series does not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 55 feet in the 1980s, 35 in the 1990s, 25 in the 2000s, 18 in the 2010s, and 31 in the 2020s. Those measurements come from different wells and conditions, so the change should not be treated as a site-specific trend. It does support checking current records rather than relying on an old well log.

sections.heading: Who drilled around Silt, and when
sections.html:
Permit history is substantial. The records include 5 permits from the 1950s, 45 from the 1960s, 197 from the 1970s, 314 from the 1980s, 675 from the 1990s, 528 from the 2000s, 197 from the 2010s and 164 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Most use is domestic or household at 77%, followed by monitoring at 14%, stock at 7% and irrigation at 4%.

Shelton Drilling Corporation, listed with Shelton, Wayne, appears most often with 785 records. Collins Drilling Co, listed with Collins, F. E. “Bodie,” has 129, and Stoneman Drilling, listed with Stoneman, Frank, has 114. These records identify historical activity, not a recommendation or proof that a company is available for a new project.

sections.heading: What a new Silt well may cost
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground at $50 to $75 per foot. At the 116-foot median depth, the drilled hole calculates to about $5,800 to $8,700. That is only the hole, not a ready-to-use water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $11,800 to $20,700 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or unexpected formation conditions can change the bid. Ask the driller to separate footage, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical work, testing and permit-related work. Comparing the proposal with nearby constructed well logs is more useful than comparing a single low per-foot price.

sections.heading: Silt risks to check before you build
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The records include 2% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, and some wells may not have a reported yield at all. Fractured-bedrock settings can be unpredictable, so a dry hole or a lower-than-expected production rate remains a possibility even near a productive well. Confirm the well’s construction, pump test and maintenance history.

Environmental due diligence also deserves attention. Within about 10 miles, the map includes 380 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 47 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped locations do not prove contamination at your property. Test the water, review nearby site information and check septic setbacks, drainage, building envelopes and access for drilling and future repairs before closing or starting construction.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Silt, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Silt is 116 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 180 feet, and 57% are between 100 and 300 feet. Some wells are deeper: the 90th-percentile depth is 240 feet and the deepest record is 750 feet. Your lot may differ with local geology.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Silt?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 116-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $5,800 to $8,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $11,800 to $20,700. Access, casing and actual depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Silt wells produce?
faq.a: Reported wells have a 14.0 gallons-per-minute median yield, with the middle half between 5.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-eight percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. However, 18% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 2% report under 1, so request the actual yield test and recovery information for the property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Silt, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 380 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 47 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well water, review nearby environmental information and inspect the well construction before using it for household drinking water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Silt?
faq.a: The recorded decade medians do not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 55 feet in the 1980s, 35 in the 1990s, 25 in the 2000s, 18 in the 2010s and 31 in the 2020s. Because the measurements come from different wells and conditions, check current water levels and pumping behavior at the specific property.
